module_summary:
Publish the document device's true capacity into the store root, from the host.

Runs on the host, never in a container: the point is to record a statvfs taken
where it is trustworthy. Docker Desktop answers statvfs on a ``/Volumes`` bind
mount with the macOS root volume, and here that volume happens to be within 1%
of the external disk's total size while differing by ~320 GiB of free space, so
capacity alone cannot detect the substitution. Workers read this file instead of
their own reading and refuse to run when it is missing or stale.

Depends only on the standard library so it can run under the host interpreter
without the project's virtualenv.

    python3 -m scrapper.commands.publish_document_store_capacity         --root "/Volumes/My Passport/passport/trading-ai" --loop 300

module_summary:
Unattended refresh of the exchange universe, with a retry ladder.

Everything before this plan step was operator-triggered. Turning it on is only
safe because C1 rejects a bad file before it can rewrite state, C2 needs a streak
of absences to remove a security, C3 refuses to overwrite an operator's row, and
C6 reports zero open conflicts. This module adds the one remaining thing: a clock,
and a ledger of what it did.

The design rule is that a failure never degrades the universe. An attempt that
cannot fetch, or whose file the guard rejects, leaves the last accepted snapshot
exactly where it was and schedules a retry. Only after the final attempt is a
dataset recorded as unrefreshed, and that exits non-zero — a day on which an
exchange published nothing is a fact an operator has to see, not a silent no-op.

The scheduling logic is a pure function of an injected clock and fetcher, so the
retry ladder is tested without APScheduler, a network or a real day passing.

module_summary:
NSE symbol-change and company-name-change files.

These files are the only evidence that keeps a renamed security the same durable
security. Names alone never merge or split a company; a change is applied only
when it resolves to an exchange key already present in the registry.
first_action: Keep source parser/adapter boundary initially
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

module_summary:
The one place that says what an exchange dataset is and where it comes from.

Before this registry the same facts lived in four modules: the dataset tuples in
`security_master.py`, `corporate_changes.py` and `result_filings.py`, the row
floors in `config.py`, and the URLs in a Compose file and a README. Automation
needs them in one structure so a scheduler can ask "which datasets refresh on a
trading day, and what do I fetch for each" without hard-coding an answer.

The registry holds configuration only: no network, no database, no parsing. Every
default URL is still re-validated through `validate_exchange_dataset_url` before
it is fetched, so being listed here grants a URL nothing.
first_action: Keep source parser/adapter boundary initially
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

module_summary:
Official NSE/BSE financial-result filing feeds.

A filing carries the reporting period, the consolidated/standalone scope and the
broadcast instant. Those three facts are what make result discovery incremental:
only filings broadcast after the stored watermark are new, and only a period
that advances beyond accepted state creates collection work.
first_action: Keep source parser/adapter boundary initially
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

module_summary:
Source-faithful parsing of the official NSE and BSE security masters.

The masters are the universe of record. A company enters the pipeline because an
exchange lists its security, not because a screen happened to show it.
first_action: Keep source parser/adapter boundary initially
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

module_summary:
Snapshot-level acceptance rules for one dated exchange file.

Per-row rejection already keeps a malformed row out of the registry. It cannot
see a file that parsed perfectly but is the wrong file: a truncated publication,
a half-written export, a reshaped report. Those pass row by row and then rewrite
current state, so a whole snapshot is judged before anything is applied.

Pure functions only: no database, no network, no clock of its own. The caller
supplies the measured facts, the prior accepted baseline and the thresholds, and
gets back a verdict it can store verbatim. Every failing rule is reported, not
just the first, so one run tells an operator everything that is wrong.
first_action: Keep source parser/adapter boundary initially
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

module_summary:
Deterministic delimited-file reading shared by the exchange adapters.

Columns are resolved from header evidence, never from fixed offsets, except for
the officially headerless NSE change files, which declare an explicit versioned
column contract instead. Every row keeps its exact source cells so a rejected
row can be reviewed against the immutable snapshot it came from.
first_action: Keep source parser/adapter boundary initially
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

C1 judges a whole dated file before it may rewrite current state, C2 requires a
streak of absences before a security stops being present, and C3 keeps an

first_action: Retain regression anchor; group by capability later
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

module_summary:
Offline tests for compressed sources and the dataset registry (C4).

Neither adds behaviour on its own. Together they are what lets a scheduler ask
"what do I fetch for this dataset" without a URL being hard-coded in a Compose
file, and what lets a gzipped report be parsed while the stored evidence stays
byte-identical to what the exchange served.
first_action: Retain regression anchor; group by capability later
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

module_summary:
Offline tests for the combined MII security file (C5).

The file carries NSE-listed and BSE-exclusive securities in one table, so every
row has to say which it is; nothing is allowed to default to an exchange. It is
also a *partial* master — it lists neither exchange's SME segment — which is why
absence sweeps are scoped to what a file is authoritative for rather than to
whatever it happens to contain.
first_action: Retain regression anchor; group by capability later
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

module_summary:
Offline tests for the first-run reconciliation report (C6).

The report exists to answer one question before automation is turned on: when an
official file met a hand-built registry, what matched, what is new, what went
unconfirmed, and where do they disagree. It is a gate as much as a document —
non-zero while any identity conflict is open.
first_action: Retain regression anchor; group by capability later
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

module_summary:
Offline tests for the scheduler and its retry ladder (C7).

An injected clock and a stub fetcher stand in for the schedule and the network,
so the ladder is exercised without APScheduler, a network or a day passing. The
property under test throughout is that a failed attempt costs nothing: the last
accepted snapshot stays exactly where it was, and the run says so.
first_action: Retain regression anchor; group by capability later
coverage: static AST and dependency inventory; detailed flow tracing is described in the review

module_summary:
Human-readable terminal rendering of collected and derived trading data.

All functions are read-only. They take an open sqlite3.Connection and return a
block of text ready to print, so the CLI layer stays a thin dispatch wrapper.

Financial sections are rendered as full period matrices (line items down, one
column per reporting period) so quarter-on-quarter and year-on-year movement is
readable at a glance, matching how the source presents them.
